questions.q: Why do designers work in a design team rather than individually on a complex project?
options: Working in a team removes the need for a project schedule or budget
No single person has every skill a complex project needs, so a team pools specialists' expertise to produce a better outcome
Teams guarantee a faster outcome because every member does the same tasks
A team means only one person has to be accountable for the result
questions.explanation: A design team is a group working toward a common goal; its core advantage is combining skills no individual possesses — an industrial designer, engineer, ergonomist and marketer pooling expertise. Teams are also used to generate ideas, solve problems, gather consumer reactions and support each other.

questions.q: Which of the following options best describes the features of a collaborative design team?
options: Leader directed, common skills among the group, responsive to feedback
Leader directed, various fields of professional expertise, responsive to feedback
Shared understanding of the project, common skills among the team, cooperative decision-making process
Shared understanding of the project, various fields of professional expertise, cooperative decision-making process
questions.explanation: A collaborative team shares a common goal (shared understanding of the project), brings together varied professional expertise rather than common skills, and decides cooperatively. The options naming 'common skills' are wrong because the whole point of a team is to combine different specialists.

questions.q: What is the main role of the team leader or project manager in a design team?
options: To complete the most technical tasks so other members don't have to
To coordinate the work and ensure that effective, agreed communication happens
To take sole responsibility for the project so members aren't accountable
To choose distractor-free ideas before the team brainstorms
questions.explanation: Most teams have a leader or project manager who coordinates the work and, importantly, ensures communication happens — they make sure the methods and timeline are agreed by all. Accountability is not theirs alone: every member is responsible for the project's completion.

questions.q: A design team works best when
options: tasks are allocated to individuals based on expertise.
the designer’s work flow is structured and organised.
design teams work in direct competition with each other.
team members always work independently towards a goal.
questions.explanation: Clearly defined roles divide the work by skill, allocating tasks to the members best suited to them — this prevents duplication and gaps. 'Always work independently' contradicts collaboration, where interdependent specialists must coordinate.

questions.q:
A web design company has introduced a collaborative design approach.

Which of the following is likely to take place?
options: Team members multi-task in each project.
A project manager directs the development of ideas.
Each design project is allocated to all team members.
Team members work together to discuss and share ideas.
questions.explanation: Collaboration means specialists working together to discuss, generate and share ideas toward a common goal — this is where individual creativity becomes collective. A single manager dictating ideas, or allocating every project to everyone, is the opposite of genuine collaboration.

questions.q: The episode summarises the factors of successful collaboration as the 'four C's'. Which set correctly lists them?
options: Cost, competition, conflict, control
Common goals, clear roles, communication, commitment
Creativity, consumer, cost, criteria
Coordination, copyright, consultation, completion
questions.explanation: The hook is the four C's — Common goals shared by all, Clear roles and tasks, sound agreed Communication, and Commitment to the goals — resting on a foundation of skilled members who respect each other and use authority fairly. It turns the exam's 'identify the factors' question into a structured answer.

questions.q: From memory: list at least four factors that contribute to successful work and collaboration in a design team.
keyPoints: Clearly defined common goals shared by all members (so the team pulls in one direction).
Clearly defined roles and tasks for each member (so work isn't duplicated or dropped).
Sound, agreed communication strategies (so information flows and problems surface early).
Commitment and accountability from everyone, plus skilled members who respect each other and use authority fairly.
questions.explanation: If you named the four C's — common goals, clear roles, communication, commitment — plus skilled members and respect, grade yourself Good or Easy. The trap is vague effort words like 'everyone works together'; the marker wants the specific structural factors.

questions.q: In your own words: why is communication essential within a design team?
keyPoints: A team is made of members with different skills working on interdependent tasks, so they must share information continually to coordinate.
Effective, agreed communication ensures everyone understands the goals and their tasks, and lets problems be raised and solved early before they become costly.
It keeps the project on schedule, which is why the team leader ensures the methods and a timeline are agreed by all.
Without it, members work in isolation and their contributions fail to fit together.
questions.explanation: The insight is that communication is what turns separate specialists into one team. If you linked interdependent tasks, early problem-solving and an agreed timeline, mark it Good or Easy.

questions.q: Describe how communication between members of a design team is supported by technology.
questions.modelAnswer: Improved capacity and capabilities of technology support communication between team members by allowing a greater volume and diversity of information to be shared quickly and conveniently from any location. Access to more information in a variety of formats speeds up the team's decision making, resulting in design solutions developed at a much greater rate and with more skilled people involved in the process.

criteria.descriptor: Provides characteristics and features of how technology supports the communication between members of a design team
Sketches in general terms how technology supports the communication between members of a design team
Identifies or provides general information of how technology supports communication when designing

questions.explanation: Link to the episode's agreed communication methods — face-to-face and video meetings, email, online forums, and shared digital files and collaborative software — and explain how these let interdependent specialists share information quickly from any location and decide faster.

questions.q: Describe how the changing nature of communication technologies has affected teamwork and collaborative design processes.
questions.modelAnswer: Changing communication technologies — teleconferencing and videoconferencing, email, online forums, and shared digital files and collaborative software — let team members share a greater volume and variety of information quickly from any location. This means specialists no longer need to be in the same place to collaborate: ideas and feedback can be exchanged continually, problems surfaced early, and a wider range of skilled people involved, speeding up decision making and the development of design solutions.

criteria.descriptor: Provides characteristics and features of the changing nature of communication technologies and the effects this has had on teamwork and collaborative design processes
Sketches in general terms how teamwork and/or collaborative design processes have been affected due to the changing nature of communication technologies
Identifies a feature of teamwork OR collaborative design processes

questions.explanation: The episode ties communication methods — video calls, email, online forums, shared files and collaborative software — back to the communication-technologies topic. Describe both the technologies and their effect: location-independent, continual collaboration that lets more specialists contribute and surfaces problems earlier.
